In Barshi, Kiran spent mornings at college, afternoons behind the counter of the family's seed shop, and nights with a torch over accounts textbooks. Exams started Monday. Amma's knee was getting worse and the monsoon was late, so sales were down. Kiran thought about all of it at once, all the time.
On Thursday Salma, a regular customer, paid for two bags of seed. Kiran gave her change for a hundred instead of fifty. She came back smiling and returned the extra. "You're somewhere else today."
That night Kiran filled in the practice form and wrote the wrong roll number twice. Kiran's head felt full of cotton.
Salma's words stuck. The next morning Kiran wrote a list: shop hours cut to three days till exams, a cousin to cover, one worry at a time.

qa.q: What mistake did Kiran make with Salma's change?
qa.a: Kiran gave her change for a hundred instead of fifty.

qa.q: What was Kiran feeling on the night of the wrong roll number?
qa.a: Kiran felt foggy and overloaded, head full of cotton, because exams, the shop and worries about Amma and the rain were all taking up space at once.

qa.q: Is Kiran's list a good response?
qa.a: Yes; cutting shop hours, asking a cousin to cover and taking one worry at a time frees some mental space, which should cut down the careless mistakes.

qa.q: How did Salma see Kiran that day?
qa.a: Salma noticed Kiran was distracted and "somewhere else", and responded kindly by returning the money with a smile.

grounding: It shows a student juggling exams, shop work and family worries who makes careless mistakes and feels foggy because stress uses up mental capacity.

passage:
In Porto, Ivan had three exams in five days, four evening shifts at the café near the university, and a letter about his residence permit renewal that he kept rereading at night. By Wednesday he was running on coffee and dread.
At the café he rang up a cappuccino as a latte, then forgot a table entirely. Beatriz, his shift partner, quietly fixed both. At home he emailed his statistics assignment to his economics professor.
"You look like a phone with too many apps open," Beatriz said at closing.
"I'm fine. I just need to push through."
"You're not dumb, you're full." She took his notepad and wrote three things: swap Friday shift, call the international office about the permit, exam first.
Ivan read the list twice. It was the first thing all week that let him breathe out.

qa.q: Where did Ivan send his statistics assignment?
qa.a: He emailed his statistics assignment to his economics professor.

qa.q: Why does Ivan insist he just needs to push through?
qa.a: He probably feels he should cope alone and doesn't see the mistakes as a sign of overload; admitting it might feel like weakness.

qa.q: Why does Beatriz's three-item list help?
qa.a: It takes the permit worry and an extra shift off his mind, so his limited attention can go to the exam first.

qa.q: How does Beatriz see Ivan's mistakes?
qa.a: Beatriz sees them as a sign he is overloaded, not careless or dumb, like a phone with too many apps open.

grounding: It shows a student juggling exams, work and a permit worry who makes careless mistakes because stress takes up part of his limited capacity.

By the second week of placements, the hostel corridor smelled of instant coffee and panic. Chinmay had two interviews, a final-year project review, and a phone that buzzed with updates about his grandfather in hospital back in Nagpur.
On Tuesday he submitted the project report with last semester's circuit diagram. On Wednesday he locked his room key inside twice. On Thursday he walked into the wrong interview hall and stood there, blank.
Eshaan, his roommate, found him on the hostel steps that night. "You're making mistakes you never make."
"I'm so stupid right now."
"Not stupid. You're carrying too much at once." Eshaan sat beside him. "Tell me everything that's in your head. We'll write it down."
They filled a page. Seeing it on paper, Chinmay cried a little, then circled the one task for tomorrow.

qa.q: What did Chinmay submit with the project report?
qa.a: He submitted it with last semester's circuit diagram.

qa.q: Why does Chinmay call himself stupid?
qa.a: He is shocked by mistakes he never usually makes and blames himself, not seeing that worry about his grandfather and the pile of tasks are using up his attention.

qa.q: How did writing everything down help Chinmay?
qa.a: Putting it on paper moved the load out of his head, let some feelings out, and left him with just one task for tomorrow.

qa.q: How does Eshaan see Chinmay's week?
qa.a: Eshaan sees a capable roommate who is overloaded, not stupid, and chooses to sit beside him and help instead of judging.

grounding: It shows a student juggling placements, a project and family worry who makes careless mistakes and feels foggy as stress uses up his capacity.

passage:
Dear Francis,
Sorry I missed your birthday call. My brain is soup these days. Exams all month, evening shifts at the hotel front desk, and Mai's shop has been slow, so I keep checking its accounts at midnight.
This week I did three stupid things. I booked two families into the same room at the hotel, and the manager had to sort it out. I wrote my roll number wrong on Monday's accounts paper and had to run to the exam office. And yesterday I put sugar in the dal instead of salt. Mai, my mother, laughed, but I didn't.
I'm not careless, you know me. It's like my head is full and every new thing spills out.
Write when you can.
Samir

qa.q: What happened at the hotel this week?
qa.a: Samir booked two families into the same room, and the manager had to sort it out.

qa.q: How does Samir feel about the mistakes?
qa.a: Samir feels frustrated and a little scared, insisting "I'm not careless" while describing a head so full that new things spill out.

qa.q: What small step could Samir take to lighten the load during exams?
qa.a: Samir could ask the hotel for fewer shifts this month and pick one fixed time to check the shop accounts instead of every midnight, freeing some room in a crowded mind.

qa.q: What might Mai have been thinking when she laughed at the sweet dal?
qa.a: She probably laughed to ease the moment, but may also have noticed how stretched and tired Samir is, and felt worried.

passage: Lakshmi, you asked what that November was like. Honestly? Fog. I had semester exams, four online tutoring sessions a night to help at home since Baba lost his job, and a head full of "what if we can't pay the hostel fee". I thought I was managing. Then the mistakes started. I uploaded my cousin's birthday video instead of my lab report. In the circuits quiz I wrote milliamps where it should have been amps, on every single answer. One night I taught a Class 8 boy the wrong formula for area, and his mother messaged me the next day. I'm Bidisha, the girl who used to find everyone else's errors. That November I couldn't find my own. It wasn't that I didn't know the stuff. There just wasn't room left in my head.

qa.q: What did Bidisha upload instead of the lab report?
qa.a: Her cousin's birthday video.

qa.q: Why does Bidisha say it wasn't that she didn't know the stuff?
qa.a: She knew the material, but worry about money and too many jobs filled her mind, so there was no room left to catch errors 😔

qa.q: What could Bidisha have tried that November to clear some of the fog?
qa.a: She could have spoken to her tutor or a college counsellor about the pressure, dropped a tutoring session or two during exams, and used a short checklist before submitting work.

qa.q: How might the mother of the Class 8 boy see Bidisha's mistake?
qa.a: She would likely be worried about her son's homework and may have doubted the tutor, without knowing how stretched Bidisha was.

grounding: A student recalls how exams, night work and money worries used up her mental space and led to careless mistakes.

Varun offered to swap his Saturday shift with hers so she could sleep and call home.

passage: In the week of his semester exams, Asif was also delivering food on his scooter every evening in Hyderabad, and his parents were arguing on the phone about his younger brother's school fees. On Monday he locked himself out of the room twice. On Tuesday he submitted his lab report with last year's file attached. On Wednesday he walked into the wrong exam hall and sat down before someone asked for his hall ticket. That night Pranav found him staring into the fridge, holding the milk and a pen, unsure why he had either. "Bro, you're running on empty," Pranav said. Asif laughed, then his eyes stung. "I'm not careless. I'm just full." They sat on the floor and wrote everything on one page: exams, shifts, the home stuff. Asif took Thursday off deliveries and emailed the professor about the report.

"Jaya, you've written 'total' as 'totla' three times."
"Have I?" Jaya stared at the page. "Pranav, I don't even know what I'm doing. I've got the audit exam Monday, my internship report due Tuesday, and Amma called to say the landlord's raising the rent."
"Okay."
"And I got the balance sheet wrong. Twice. I've done this a hundred times."
"Because you're doing four things in your head at once."
"I'm just being stupid."
"You're not stupid. You're full." Pranav pulled out a sheet of paper. "Write it all down. Every worry. Then we pick one."
She wrote: exam, report, rent, sleep.
"Now, which one is today?"
"The exam."
"Then the rest waits on the paper." He tapped it. "Do one balance sheet. Slowly."
Her third try balanced.

qa.q: How did Jaya misspell 'total'?
qa.a: She wrote it as 'totla'.

qa.q: Why does Jaya think she's 'just being stupid'?
qa.a: Jaya feels frustrated and ashamed at getting a familiar balance sheet wrong, not seeing that the exam, the report and the rent worry are crowding her mind.

qa.q: What did Pranav suggest, and why did it help?
qa.a: Writing every worry on paper and picking one for today, which frees up her mind so the balance sheet finally balances.

qa.q: How does Pranav see Jaya's mistakes?
qa.a: Pranav sees a friend who is full, not stupid, and helps her put the worries down.

Last semester was the worst. I had three exams in one week, my evening shift at the call centre, and my grandmother was in hospital. I kept thinking about all of it at once.

In my accounts exam I copied a number wrong in the first line and the whole answer fell apart. At work I sent a customer the wrong form twice. I even left my hostel room keys inside the lock.

My roommate Rehana said, "You're not careless, you're carrying too much." I didn't believe her at first. But when I made a list of everything in my head, it filled a whole page.

I'm Mahima. I learnt my brain isn't endless. When worry takes up space, there's less left for the exam.

Faculty mentor's note, Tuesday.

Sachin came to see me after failing a lab quiz he would normally pass. He looked exhausted. He told me he's working nights at his uncle's shop, preparing for three exams, and worrying about his younger sister Rekha, who has been unwell.

He said, "I read the question and it slips away. I made silly mistakes, like labelling the wrong axis." He seemed embarrassed.

I explained that when a lot is on your mind, there's less room for thinking, and it's not laziness. I helped him list his deadlines and we moved one lab report by a week. I also gave him the number for the student counselling service, and he booked an appointment before leaving my room.

qa.q: What mistake did Sachin mention making?
qa.a: Labelling the wrong axis.

qa.q: How was Sachin feeling when he talked to the mentor?
qa.a: He seemed exhausted and embarrassed, worried that the mistakes meant he was lazy.

qa.q: What steps did the mentor take to help?
qa.a: The mentor explained the mistakes weren't laziness, helped list deadlines, moved one lab report and gave the counselling number, which Sachin used that day.

qa.q: How might Rekha be affected if she learned her brother was struggling?
qa.a: Rekha might feel worried or guilty, since her illness is part of what he's carrying.

grounding: A mentor notes a student juggling exams, work and worries who makes careless mistakes because stress fills mental capacity.

passage:
Thursday, midnight

I put salt in my tea this morning. Salt. Amandeep laughed so hard she had to sit down.

Then in the stats test I skipped a whole question without noticing. At the library desk where I work part-time, I stamped the wrong return date on five books. And I forgot to call home.

It's the internship applications, the test, the library hours, and the fight with my roommate. My brain feels like a phone with forty apps open.

I'm not stupid. I know that. I'm just full.

Tomorrow: write everything on one list, pick three things, and tell the library supervisor I need one lighter shift this week. — Indu

qa.a: Salt.

qa.q: How does Indu feel at midnight on Thursday?
qa.a: Indu feels overwhelmed and foggy, like a phone with forty apps open, but also knows the problem isn't stupidity.

qa.a: Amandeep probably found it funny at first, though she might also notice Indu seems unusually scattered.

In Tezpur, Sonali's days had become a blur. Morning: classes at the college. Afternoon: minding the family's grocery shop while her father was away. Evening: helping her grandmother with dinner and medicines. Night: studying for the semester exams.
On Tuesday she gave a customer change for a five-hundred note when he'd paid with a hundred. On Wednesday she forgot to submit her exam form until Kavitha reminded her at 4:55. On Thursday she put sugar in the dal.
"I'm becoming stupid," she told Kavitha, near tears.
"You're doing four jobs," Kavitha said. "Your head is full. Anyone's would slip."
They sat at the shop counter and made a plan. Kavitha's mother could mind the shop two afternoons a week. Sonali would write every deadline on the calendar by the till. And she'd tell her father about the change mistake when he called, instead of hiding it.

In the week before his engineering finals in Johannesburg, Bilal was working night shifts at a warehouse, sending money home, and lying awake worrying about his younger brother's school fees.
On Monday he missed a minus sign and got a whole practice problem wrong. On Tuesday he left his student card on the bus. On Wednesday he forgot Lindiwe's birthday, though she was his closest friend on the course.
He found her in the library to apologise, and to his own surprise his eyes filled. "I'm not like this. I'm careful. My head is just fog."
Lindiwe pushed her notes aside. "Bilal, you're carrying three lives. Of course things are falling out."
She made a list with him: tell the warehouse he needs the week off, study in the mornings when his head is clearest, and book the student support office about the fees worry. "One thing at a time," she said. "The birthday can wait."

qa.q: Where did Bilal leave his student card?
qa.a: Bilal left his student card on the bus.

qa.q: How did Bilal feel when he apologised to Lindiwe?
qa.a: Bilal felt ashamed and overwhelmed, near tears, sure he was usually careful but now foggy.

qa.q: What plan did Lindiwe help Bilal make?
qa.a: Asking the warehouse for the week off, studying in the mornings when his head is clearest, and booking the student support office about the fees.

The campus bookshop was packed during winter fest week, and Yash was working the evening till between mock exams. His phone kept lighting up with messages from home about Nanaji's hospital tests.
He gave a customer change for two hundred instead of five hundred. He shelved the chemistry guides under history. At seven he noticed he had written yesterday's date on the delivery sheet. Twice.
"Yash, the stapler is in your hand," Hafsa said gently, as he searched the drawer for it.
He laughed, but it came out shaky. "My head's like a browser with forty tabs open."
Hafsa, the shift supervisor, pulled out a stool. "Sit for five minutes. Drink some water. Then just the till, nothing else, until eight."
He sat, pressing his palms against his eyes. The noise of the fest drifted in from the lawn.

qa.q: What was Yash searching the drawer for?
qa.a: The stapler, which was in his hand.

qa.q: What was Yash feeling during his shift, and how can you tell?
qa.a: He felt overwhelmed and anxious, shown by the careless mistakes, the shaky laugh and his line about a browser with forty tabs open.

qa.q: How did Hafsa lighten Yash's load?
qa.a: She gave him a short break with water and then narrowed his job to just the till until eight.
